etymology: Greek mna, from Hebrew māneh (a fixed weight or sum); equal to 100 drachmas (approximately 100 days’ wages for a laborer); the unit of weight-and-currency used in the Parable of the Pounds (Luke 19:12-27). The KJV renders mna as pound; modern translations often use mina.
biblical_def: The mina (KJV pound) is the Greek unit of weight-and-currency equal to 100 drachmas, approximately 100 days’ wages for a laborer—a substantial sum, but smaller than the talent (60 minas) of the parallel parable in Matthew 25. The mina appears most significantly in the Parable of the Pounds in Luke 19:12-27, which Christ delivered as He was making His final approach to Jerusalem before His passion. A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return. And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come. Each servant received one mina (in contrast to the talents-parable of Matt 25 where the servants received different amounts according to ability). On the nobleman’s return, two servants reported their faithful work: one had gained ten minas with his one mina; another had gained five minas with his one mina; both were commended and given authority over cities corresponding to their gain. A third had hid his mina in a napkin out of fear, and his mina was taken away and given to the servant with ten. The structural lessons of the parable are several. First, equal distribution: every servant received the same one mina, against the talents-parable’s differentiated distribution—suggesting that the mina-parable focuses on faithfulness with what is commonly entrusted (the gospel, the Word, the basic resources of Christian discipleship) rather than on differentiated gifts. Second, occupy till I come: the explicit charge to put the mina to active use in the nobleman’s absence—the active stewardship of the deposit until the Master’s return. Third, proportionate reward: the servant who gained ten minas was given authority over ten cities; the one who gained five over five cities; the reward in the kingdom is proportionate to the faithfulness in the present age. Fourth, the judgment on the wicked servant: thou wicked servant, out of thine own mouth will I judge thee—his own rationalization (the master is austere, reaping what he did not sow) is turned against him; if he believed that, he should at least have put the mina in the bank for interest. Fifth, the dramatic conclusion involving the citizens who sent a message after the nobleman, we will not have this man to reign over us, and whose end is to be slain before him (v. 27)—the parable’s reckoning includes not only the servants of the household but the wider citizenry who rejected the king’s authority. The mina-parable therefore weaves together stewardship of the common deposit, proportionate reward in the kingdom, and the comprehensive accounting at the King’s return that includes both the faithful and unfaithful servants and the rebellious citizens alike.

corruption_summary: The Parable of the Pounds is corrupted, on one side, by sentimentalized readings that have removed the judgment-on-the-wicked-servant and judgment-on-the-rebellious-citizens conclusions (treating it as a gentle stewardship lesson without its sober eschatological reckoning)—and on the other by certain post-millennial readings that have read the parable’s structural details as endorsing particular political programs of dominion, against the parable’s actual focus on faithful occupation-with-deposit until the King’s return.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentimentalized reading reduces the Parable of the Pounds to a gentle stewardship lesson, focusing on the good servants’ commendation and removing the parable’s sober conclusions: the wicked servant’s mina taken away and given to the faithful, and the rebellious citizens’ being brought hither and slain before the returning king. The parable as Christ told it has both registers—commendation and judgment. The faithful are honored proportionately; the unfaithful is exposed by his own words; the rebels are dealt with finally. To preach the parable’s commendation without its judgment-conclusion is to truncate Christ’s teaching and to present a softer Christ than the one Luke 19 actually gives. The recovery is the recovery of the whole parable: the stewardship of the deposit, the proportionate reward of the faithful, the exposure of the unfaithful, and the comprehensive reckoning at the King’s return that includes both household and citizenry.

The opposite corruption is the post-millennial-dominionist over-extension that has read the parable’s structural details (the nobleman receiving the kingdom; the servants given authority over cities; the rebellious citizens slain) as endorsing particular political programs of Christian dominion over earthly cities and nations. The parable is set in the context of Christ’s approach to Jerusalem and is partly addressed to the disciples’ misunderstanding that the kingdom of God should immediately appear (Luke 19:11). Its focus is the King’s departure to receive the kingdom, the saints’ faithful stewardship of His deposit in His absence, and the comprehensive reckoning at His return. The cities-of-reward in the parable belong to the kingdom-coming, not to a present-age political program. Recover both ends. Refuse the sentimentalized reading that removes the judgment-conclusions, and refuse the dominionist over-extension that treats the parable as endorsing present-age political programs. The biblical Parable of the Pounds calls every saint to faithful active stewardship of what the King has entrusted, with the King’s return as the day of reckoning when commendation and judgment are both dispensed.

etymology: Middle English ferthing, a fourth-part; the smallest English coin (one-fourth of a penny). The KJV uses farthing for two different small Greek coins: the Roman quadrans (one-fourth of an as; 1/256 of a denarius—Matt 5:26; Mark 12:42) and the Greek assarion (1/16 of a denarius—Matt 10:29; Luke 12:6).
biblical_def: The farthing in the KJV renders two different small coins of the first-century Roman world: the quadrans (one-fourth of an as, approximately 1/256 of a denarius, the smallest copper coin in everyday circulation) and the assarion (a small bronze coin worth 1/16 of a denarius). Both are small denominations, used in the Gospels to illustrate either the smallest unit of debt or the cheapest of items. The supreme uses are several. Matthew 5:26: Christ’s warning at the end of the Sermon on the Mount’s anger-and-reconciliation passage: verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing. The context is the man who has angered his brother and not been reconciled; if the matter reaches the magistrate, the debt-prison will hold him until the entire debt is paid down to the smallest copper. The reference is rhetorical: the smallest farthing is the lowest unit, the absolute exact-and-complete amount. Mark 12:42 (paralleled in Luke 21:2): the widow’s two mites which make a farthing—the smallest two coins available, which together made the smallest copper coin in higher denomination. Matt 10:29 and Luke 12:6: are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. The sparrows here are sold at the cheapest possible rate—two birds for a small bronze coin—and Christ’s teaching is that even at this nearly-worthless commercial valuation, the Father’s providence extends to every individual bird; how much more then to His children. The biblical doctrine of the farthing therefore has structural pastoral substance across multiple registers. First, the legal-debt register: the uttermost farthing must be paid; God’s justice is exact and complete, and the debt of sin is not partially-paid but fully-paid (Christ’s cry It is finished [tetelestai, paid in full] is the gospel-answer to the demand for the uttermost farthing). Second, the small-gift register: the widow’s two mites totaling one farthing is measured by Christ as more than the rich men’s substantial gifts because of the proportion and cost (her gift was all she had, theirs was overflow). Third, the providence register: the sparrows sold for a farthing are individually known to the Father, and the saint’s value to Him is incomparably greater. The smallest coin in everyday circulation becomes, in Christ’s hands, the carrier of teaching that ranges from the exactness of divine justice to the tenderness of divine providence over every detail of the saint’s life.

corruption_summary: The farthing-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the loss of the small-coin precision in modern translations (which often substitute the colorless cent or penny for the KJV’s farthing, losing the carefully-distinguished quadrans-vs-assarion of the original), and by the consequent loss of the structural pastoral substance that runs through the small-coin uses across the Gospels.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern translations have generally simplified the small-coin vocabulary, substituting cent, penny, or generic small coin for the KJV’s careful farthing, mite, penny, pound, stater, etc. The simplification is grammatically defensible (modern English does not maintain a precise multi-tier hierarchy of small coins as the first-century Roman East did) but pastorally costly. The KJV’s farthing covers two distinct Greek coins (quadrans and assarion) at carefully-distinguished biblical moments; the loss of the precision flattens what Christ’s teaching is doing. The uttermost farthing of Matt 5:26 carries a force the colorless last penny equivalents miss; two sparrows for a farthing of Matt 10:29 carries the precise rate the modern equivalents soften. The recovery is the recovery of the precision: read the KJV with attention to its careful coin-vocabulary, and the pastoral substance the small-coin teaching carries comes through with full force.

The structural pastoral substance that runs through the small-coin uses is itself worth noting. Christ’s use of the smallest coins-of-everyday-life as the carriers of teaching about divine justice (the uttermost farthing of exact reckoning), divine providence (the sparrows the Father sees fall), and disciple-faithfulness (the widow’s two mites worth more than the rich men’s talents) is itself a deep pattern. The kingdom of heaven values rightly what the world values cheaply; the smallest coin matters in the divine accounting; the smallest gift, given in faith from the smallest means, is weightier in heaven than the largest gift given from abundance. The recovery of the small-coin teaching is therefore the recovery of an entire register of Christ’s pastoral instruction—a register that the modern simplification of vocabulary has often quietly muted.

etymology: Plural of penny; the KJV renders the Greek dēnarion (denarius) as penny, with pence as the plural. The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin, approximately one day’s wage for an ordinary laborer in the first-century Mediterranean world.
biblical_def: Pence is the plural of penny—the KJV’s rendering of the Greek dēnarion (denarius), the standard Roman silver coin worth approximately one day’s wage for an ordinary laborer. The denarius was the most commonly-used larger denomination in first-century Palestine, the coin of ordinary commerce and standard payments. Several structural biblical moments turn on the denarius. First, the parable of the laborers in the vineyard (Matt 20:1-16). The householder agrees with the laborers hired at dawn for a penny a day (a fair daily wage); throughout the day he hires additional workers; at the day’s end he pays each one a penny, beginning with those hired last. The first-hired murmur that they received the same as those who worked only one hour; the householder responds that he has done them no wrong (a penny is a fair daily wage and what was agreed), that he is free to do with his own what he will, that the last shall be first and the first last. The parable teaches the sovereignty of God in dispensing reward, the equality of access to the kingdom, and the impropriety of comparing one’s portion with another’s. Second, the question about tribute to Caesar (Matt 22:15-22; Mark 12:13-17). The Pharisees and Herodians try to entangle Christ: is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not? Christ asks for the tribute money and is brought a penny (denarius); He asks whose image and superscription are on it; they answer, Caesar’s; He concludes, render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. The penny becomes the visual aid for one of the most important political-theological teachings of the New Testament: civil obligation to the magistrate within the larger total obligation to God. Third, the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37). The Samaritan, having bound up the wounded man, brought him to the inn, and taken care of him, on the next day gave the host two pence (two denarii) with the instruction to take care of the wounded man and the promise that whatsoever the host spent more, the Samaritan would repay at his return. The two pence—two days’ wages—is a substantial advance for ongoing care, illustrating the costly practical love the parable models. Fourth, the parable of the unmerciful servant’s fellow-servant (Matt 18:28): the forgiven servant grabs his fellow-servant by the throat for a debt of an hundred pence—a substantial sum (100 days’ wages) but trivial compared to his own forgiven debt of 10,000 talents. The pence-amount in the parable is the proportionate small-debt against the forgiven larger-debt, illustrating the ingratitude of refusing to forgive minor offenses after receiving massive forgiveness.

corruption_summary: The pence-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the modern translation drift that has often substituted vague day’s wage or specific denarius for the KJV’s penny, losing the precision the KJV preserves—and by the consequent loss of pastoral attention to the precise sums Christ’s parables use (one penny, two pence, hundred pence) as carriers of theological substance.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern translations have variously rendered the Greek denarius as denarius (the technical name), day’s wage (the functional value), or silver coin (the general category). Each has its merits; each loses something the KJV’s penny preserves. The KJV-reader accustomed to the coin-vocabulary tracks the precise sums Christ’s parables use: one penny is the day’s wage of the vineyard laborer; two pence is the Samaritan’s advance to the innkeeper; an hundred pence is the small-debt against the unmerciful servant’s 10,000 talents; the penny shown to Christ in the tribute question is the standard Roman coin with Caesar’s image and superscription. The precise sums matter: the parable’s force often depends on the proportional contrast (two pence is substantial care; an hundred pence is meaningful but trivial against 10,000 talents) that the modern flattening can muddy.

The deeper pastoral substance is that Christ’s parables use the precise small-and-mid-sized sums of everyday life as the carriers of teaching about justice, generosity, forgiveness, and the kingdom’s economics. The vineyard penny teaches God’s sovereign generosity in dispensing reward; the tribute penny teaches the proper rendering of civil obligation within total obligation to God; the Samaritan’s two pence teaches costly practical love; the unmerciful servant’s hundred pence teaches the obligation of the forgiven-much to forgive the small. The recovery of the coin-vocabulary is therefore not antiquarianism but the recovery of a register of teaching that runs through the Gospels with concrete pastoral substance. Christ teaches in the currency of His hearers; the contemporary reader who learns the coin-precision hears the parables in the register Christ used.

etymology: Greek statēr, “a standard,” from histēmi (to stand). A Greek silver coin equal to four drachmas or two didrachmas (two temple-tax half-shekels); the coin found by Peter in the fish’s mouth in Matt 17:27.
biblical_def: The stater is the Greek silver coin worth four drachmas or two didrachmas—exactly the amount needed to pay the temple tax for two persons. The word appears once in the New Testament, in one of the most singular incidents of Christ’s earthly ministry: the temple-tax episode of Matthew 17:24-27. The narrative: when Christ and the disciples have come to Capernaum, the collectors of the temple half-shekel tax (the didrachma) approach Peter and ask: doth not your master pay tribute? Peter answers, yes. When Peter comes into the house, Christ anticipates him and asks: what thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers? Peter saith unto him, Of strangers. Jesus saith unto him, Then are the children free. The reasoning is christologically deep: Christ is the Son of the King whose temple-tax is being collected; the Son of God owes no temple-tax to His own Father’s house. But Christ chooses not to claim the exemption: notwithstanding, lest we should offend them, go thou to the sea, and cast an hook, and take up the fish that first cometh up; and when thou hast opened his mouth, thou shalt find a piece of money (a stater): that take, and give unto them for me and thee. Several structural features mark the incident. First, the Christology: Christ is the Son who has no tax-obligation to His Father’s house, the One greater than the temple, the Lord of the Sabbath who is also the Lord of the temple. Second, the principled non-offense: He chooses not to claim His exemption, lest the still-blinded collectors stumble at His teaching by misunderstanding the refusal. Third, the divine knowledge: He knows the exact coin is in the mouth of the exact first fish Peter will catch. Fourth, the precision of the sum: a single stater is exactly the amount for two temple-taxes (one for Christ, one for Peter). Fifth, the lesson on Christian liberty and the avoidance of offense: there are matters in which the Christian has the right to insist on his exemption or liberty but chooses not to, lest the weak be offended (1 Cor 8-10; Rom 14 develop the principle Christ models here). Sixth, the providence-demonstration: the fish, the coin in the fish’s mouth, the timing of Peter’s catch, the precision of the sum—all coordinate as evidence of Christ’s divine knowledge and provision. The stater of Matthew 17:27 is therefore one of the most theologically loaded single coins in the Bible, carrying Christology (the Son’s exemption), the doctrine of voluntarily-foregone-liberty (the non-offense principle), and a vivid demonstration of Christ’s divine knowledge and providence over the sea’s creatures.

corruption_summary: The stater-incident is corrupted, on one side, by the rationalist-critical tradition that has treated the fish-with-the-coin narrative as a quaint legendary detail rather than as the substantive demonstration of Christ’s divine knowledge and providence that Matthew records—and on the other by the loss of the deeper Christological-and-liberty teaching that the incident embodies in much contemporary preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The rationalist-critical tradition has often treated the fish-with-the-coin narrative as a quaint legendary detail or as a folktale parallel to other ancient miracle stories, rather than as the substantive demonstration of Christ’s divine knowledge and providence that Matthew records as historical event. The reading misses what Matthew is doing. The narrative is told with precise detail (Capernaum, the temple-tax collectors, Peter’s exchange with Christ, the principled reasoning, the specific instructions to cast a hook and take the first fish, the exact-amount coin in the fish’s mouth, the use for both Christ and Peter) consistent with an actual event being reported. The Christological substance depends on the actuality: Christ knows the coin is in the fish; the providence coordinates the fish’s catch with the moment of need; the sum is precisely calibrated; the Christ who can do this is the Christ whose Sonship-exemption to the temple-tax is theologically grounded in His actual deity. The recovery is the recovery of the historical-realist reading: Matthew records an actual event demonstrating Christ’s actual divine knowledge and providence over creation.

The opposite corruption is the loss of the deeper Christological-and-liberty teaching the incident embodies. Christ’s reasoning—then are the children free—is a theological claim of immense weight: the Son is exempt from His Father’s house-tax because of His Sonship; the disciples, in some derivative sense, share the exemption as those whom He has made sons together with Himself. And yet Christ voluntarily forgoes the exemption to avoid offense to the weak. The doctrine has direct application to Christian liberty and the non-offense principle that Paul develops at length in 1 Cor 8-10 and Rom 14: there are matters in which the believer has the legal-or-doctrinal right to insist on his liberty but chooses not to, lest the weak be offended or the witness damaged. Christ Himself models the principle at Capernaum. The contemporary believer often misses the Christological substance (treating the fish-and-coin as a quaint miracle) and the liberty-application (treating Paul’s 1 Cor 8-10 teaching as abstract principle). The recovery holds them together: the Son who is exempt and yet voluntarily forgoes the exemption is the model for every saint who has Christian liberty in a matter and may, for the sake of avoiding offense to the weak, voluntarily decline to exercise it.

etymology: Hebrew beqa‘, “a half,” from bāqa‘ (to split, divide); a half-shekel weight, the standard amount for the half-shekel atonement-tax of Exodus 30:11-16.
biblical_def: The bekah is the Hebrew half-shekel weight (the word means literally a half), the standard amount specified for the atonement-tax every adult Israelite male paid for the support of the tabernacle’s service. Exodus 30:11-16 prescribes the doctrine: when thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them. This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD. Every one that passeth among them that are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering unto the LORD. The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when they give an offering unto the LORD, to make an atonement for your souls. The detail of the doctrine is theologically substantive. First, the equality of the atonement-payment: the rich and poor pay the same exact amount—the half-shekel ransom is the same for every soul, because every soul’s value before God is the same, and the atonement-substitute is not measured by the offerer’s means but by the soul’s objective worth. Second, the universal obligation: every adult male above twenty years pays; no one is exempt; the principle of universal liability for atonement is built into the very census-procedure. Third, the soul-language: the payment is explicitly a ransom for his soul and to make an atonement for your souls; the bekah is not generic tax-revenue but specifically substitutionary-atonement money. Fourth, the plague-prevention: the payment that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them recalls David’s later sin of numbering Israel without the atonement-payment (2 Sam 24; 1 Chr 21), which resulted in the plague that David then atoned for by buying Araunah’s threshingfloor (the site of the future temple). Fifth, the temple-service support: the half-shekel funded the ongoing service of the tabernacle (and later the temple), so that the atonement-payment of each Israelite was the financial sustenance of the sanctuary’s worship. Sixth, the typological substance. The half-shekel atonement-tax prefigured the full ransom Christ would pay for every soul: not the half-shekel of equal token-payment but the precious blood of the Lamb without blemish, paid as the once-for-all ransom that no soul could pay for itself and that perfectly redeems every soul for whom it was offered. The bekah is therefore not numismatic curiosity but the precise OT figure of the substitutionary atonement Christ Himself accomplished.

RANSOM, n. — The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for procuring the release of a forfeit; in scripture, the price of redemption for the soul, paid in OT type as the half-shekel and in substantive reality as the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).

corruption_summary: The bekah half-shekel atonement-tax is corrupted chiefly by the general loss of OT-cultic typology that has dropped its explicit Christological substance (the ransom-for-the-soul that prefigured Christ’s full ransom of every soul)—and by the inverse error of treating the equal half-shekel payment as a generic principle of equal taxation without the substantive substitutionary-atonement theology that grounds it.
corruption_paragraphs: The general loss of OT-cultic typology has dropped the bekah half-shekel atonement-tax from contemporary preaching as obscure cultic detail without operative theological substance. Yet the substance is significant. The half-shekel payment is explicitly named as a ransom for his soul; the equality of rich-and-poor payment teaches that the soul’s atonement-value is uniform; the universal obligation teaches that every soul requires atonement; the plague-prevention rationale grounds the doctrine in the LORD’s holiness against numbered souls without atonement. And the typological substance is direct: the half-shekel prefigured the full ransom Christ would pay for every soul, the precious blood of the Lamb without blemish that no human payment could substitute and that perfectly redeems every soul for whom it was offered. The recovery is the recovery of the typological reading: 1 Peter 1:18-19 is the apostolic application of the OT ransom-language, and the bekah is one of its most precise typological anchors.

The opposite corruption is the treatment of the equal half-shekel payment as a generic principle of equal-tax-rates without the substantive substitutionary-atonement theology. Some readings have taken Ex 30:15 (the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less) as authorizing flat-tax political theory or as a generic principle of equal-treatment-before-God in financial matters. The text’s actual structure is more specific. The equality is grounded not in a generic flat-tax principle but in the substitutionary-atonement reality: the soul-value is uniform; the atonement-substitute is the same for every soul; the half-shekel is not generic taxation but specifically ransom-payment. Read the equality off from the atonement-doctrine, not the atonement-doctrine off from a generic equality-of-taxation principle. The bekah’s substantive doctrine is the substitutionary atonement; the equality-of-payment is a feature of that doctrine, not the doctrine itself. Recover both ends. Refuse the loss of OT-cultic typology that drops the doctrine altogether, and refuse the over-extension that treats the bekah’s equality-of-payment as a generic political principle. The biblical bekah teaches the universal need for atonement, the uniform value of every soul before God, and the typological anticipation of the full ransom Christ would pay—the substantive substitutionary-atonement doctrine that grounds the gospel itself.

etymology: Hebrew gērāh, probably from a root meaning a grain or small object; the smallest weight unit in the Hebrew system, equal to 1/20 of a shekel of the sanctuary (approximately 0.02 oz / 0.57 g of silver).
biblical_def: The gerah is the smallest weight unit in the Hebrew system—1/20 of a shekel of the sanctuary, mentioned five times in the OT exclusively as the precise standard for measuring half-shekel, shekel, and larger weights. Exodus 30:13 prescribes the standard: this they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD. The gerah-standard is mentioned similarly in Lev 27:25; Num 3:47; 18:16; and Ezek 45:12 (Ezekiel’s prophetic temple vision specifies the standard with reference to the gerah). The structural significance of the gerah is twofold. First, the precision of biblical weights: the OT does not deal in approximations but in precisely-standardized units. The shekel of the sanctuary was a specific weight (the temple-standard), and it was reckoned in exactly twenty gerahs. The Israelite buying, selling, paying tribute, weighing-out atonement money knew exactly what a shekel weighed because the standard was set in the most easily-verifiable terms (twenty units of the smallest standard weight). Second, the smallness as standard: the smallest unit of the system was the basis of the larger units’ precision. By specifying that one shekel equals twenty gerahs, the LORD ensured that every shekel-payment could be checked against the verifiable smaller standard, and that no merchant or priest could manipulate the larger units without violating the smaller ones. The biblical-pastoral application of the gerah-precision is the wider biblical theology of just weights and measures, which the prophets repeatedly emphasize. Leviticus 19:35-36: ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure. Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt. Proverbs 11:1: a false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight. Proverbs 20:10: divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD. Amos 8:5 condemns merchants who make the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsify the balances by deceit. Micah 6:11: shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights? The gerah-standard’s precision is the basis of the prophetic ethics: the LORD’s holiness requires that every weight be just, every measure exact, every commercial transaction honest—and the very precision-standardization of the OT weights-and-measures system (with the small gerah as the verifying base) is the structural infrastructure on which the prophetic ethics depends.

webster_full: GERAH, n. — (Hebrew weight.) The smallest weight in the Hebrew system, equal to 1/20 of a shekel of the sanctuary (Ex 30:13; Lev 27:25; Num 3:47; 18:16; Ezek 45:12).

WEIGHTS AND MEASURES — The biblical doctrine of just commercial standards, prescribed in Lev 19:35-36 and Deut 25:13-16, condemned in their corruption by the prophets (Amos 8:5; Mic 6:11; Hos 12:7), and grounded in the LORD’s holiness against deceitful commerce.

corruption_summary: The gerah-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the general loss of biblical-economic ethics in much contemporary preaching, which has muted the prophetic-and-Mosaic emphasis on just weights and measures that the gerah-precision-standard underwrites; the doctrine’s recovery is the recovery of the biblical theology of honest commerce as part of the LORD’s holiness against the deceitful trading patterns of every age including the present.
corruption_paragraphs: The general loss of biblical-economic ethics in much contemporary preaching has muted the OT and prophetic emphasis on just weights and measures, of which the gerah-precision-standard is the structural foundation. The prophetic literature thunders against deceitful balances, divers weights, false measures, the making-of-the-ephah-small-and-the-shekel-great pattern of contemporary commerce. The contemporary application is direct: every age has its forms of deceitful commerce—tampered measures, misleading advertising, hidden fees, manipulated invoices, false labeling, deceptive pricing, fraudulent accounting—and the LORD’s holiness against these is no less than His holiness against the OT merchants who falsified the balances. The Christian businessman, accountant, contractor, employee, employer is bound by the same ethics that the gerah-standard underwrote in OT Israel: every weight just, every measure exact, every transaction honest, every account truly stated. The recovery is the recovery of biblical-economic ethics as part of the saint’s discipleship, with the gerah-precision-standard as the OT figure of the precision-honesty God’s holiness requires in commerce.

The deeper pastoral substance is that the LORD’s holiness extends into every detail of human life, including the smallest units of commercial measurement. The gerah was the smallest unit in the Hebrew system, and the LORD specified the larger units in terms of the smallest—ensuring that no manipulation of the larger could escape verification by the smaller. Applied today: the saint’s honesty is to extend to the smallest details of his financial life. The integrity of the larger transactions is built on the integrity of the smaller. The believer who is honest in the visible large transactions and dishonest in the small (the petty cash, the expense report, the under-the-table payment, the unreported income) has corrupted the whole, because the LORD’s holiness extends to the smallest unit and no commercial integrity is real that does not begin at the gerah-level. The contemporary recovery is the recovery of comprehensive financial integrity, all the way down to the smallest units, as part of the discipleship that responds to the holiness of the God who set the weights and measures of His people with such precision.

etymology: Hebrew qāb, “a hollow vessel,” from a root meaning to be hollow; a small dry-measure equal to approximately 1/18 of an ephah (about 2 quarts or 2.1 liters). Appears once in Scripture, at the famine of Samaria in 2 Kings 6:25.
biblical_def: The cab is a Hebrew unit of dry measure, approximately 1/18 of an ephah (about 2 quarts in volume), mentioned only once in Scripture: at the famine of Samaria during the Syrian siege under Benhadad in 2 Kings 6:25. And there was a great famine in Samaria: and, behold, they besieged it, until an ass’s head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver. The verse is one of the more grim in the OT narrative, illustrating the extremity of starvation in the besieged city: an ass’s head (normally unclean food, eaten only in desperation) sold for 80 silver pieces; a quarter-cab of dove’s dung (probably the indigestible plant-seed residue in the dung, or possibly a colloquial name for some inferior vegetable matter) sold for 5 silver pieces. The narrative continues with the most shocking incident of the famine: two women had agreed to boil and eat their children to survive; one woman boiled her son and ate him with the other; when the other woman hid her son rather than fulfilling her side of the agreement, the first appealed to the king for justice (2 Kgs 6:26-29). The king, learning the depth of the famine’s horror, tore his clothes and revealed the sackcloth he wore beneath. The cab in 2 Kings 6:25 is therefore a window into one of Scripture’s most somber narratives: the consequences of covenant unfaithfulness reaching the point of cannibalism within the besieged covenant city, with the smallest units of food sold at extortionate prices and the population reduced to eating what would never have been considered food in normal life. The narrative belongs to the larger biblical theology of covenant-curse: Deut 28:53-57 prophetically described exactly this kind of siege-cannibalism as among the most severe curses for covenant-breaking, and 2 Kings 6 records its fulfillment in the northern kingdom’s history. The cab as a unit therefore takes on, in its single biblical use, a structural-theological weight far beyond its small literal measurement: it is the measuring-unit of covenant judgment-extremity. Elisha’s subsequent prophecy in 2 Kings 7:1 (announcing the deliverance and the restoration of normal grain prices the next day) and its dramatic fulfillment through the Syrian retreat is the LORD’s answer to the famine and the demonstration that the same God who appoints siege also appoints deliverance.

FAMINE, n. — Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions; in scripture, often the consequence of covenant-unfaithfulness, with siege-famine being among the most severe of the covenant-curses prophetically described in Deut 28:53-57.

corruption_summary: The cab-narrative is corrupted in contemporary reading chiefly by being skipped past as obscure OT detail, missing the structural-covenantal substance of the famine-as-covenant-curse fulfillment and the dramatic deliverance through Elisha’s prophecy—and by the avoidance, in much contemporary preaching, of the somber siege-famine details that the OT records as the consequences of covenant unfaithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: The 2 Kings 6 narrative is widely skipped in contemporary preaching as too somber, too gruesome, too disconnected from contemporary application—ass’s heads and dove’s dung and women cannibalizing their children belong, in the contemporary preacher’s judgment, to a register of OT horror that the modern congregation should be spared. Scripture includes the narrative, however, with deliberate purpose. It demonstrates the literal fulfillment of Deut 28:53-57’s covenant-curse prophecy; it shows the consequences of sustained covenant-unfaithfulness reaching the depths of siege-famine; it sets up the contrast with Elisha’s prophesied deliverance in chapter 7. The recovery is the recovery of biblical realism about covenant-consequences. The LORD’s holiness against sustained unfaithfulness is real; the prophesied judgments are not metaphorical but actual; the OT narrative records the historical fulfillment of the warnings the law had given. The contemporary application is sober: God’s covenant-people, then and now, are not exempt from the consequences of sustained unfaithfulness, and the contemporary pastor who avoids the somber OT narratives is hiding from the saints the warnings the Lord Himself recorded for their good.

The deeper pastoral substance includes the dramatic deliverance that follows. Elisha’s prophecy in 2 Kings 7:1 announces that the very famine that has reduced the people to extremity will be reversed the next day by the LORD’s action: a measure of fine flour for a shekel, two measures of barley for a shekel, normal prices restored at the gate. The deliverance comes through the most unexpected of means: four lepers, marginalized at the city gate, discover the empty Syrian camp (the LORD having frightened the Syrians with the sound of a great army and put them to flight); they bring back the news; the city is delivered overnight; Elisha’s prophecy is fulfilled to the day. The narrative pattern is one of the OT’s most pastorally consoling: even at the depth of covenant-curse’s extremity, the LORD’s deliverance can come in an hour, through means the besieged would never have imagined. Recover the somber narrative and recover the dramatic deliverance together; the doctrine that emerges is one of God’s holiness against sustained unfaithfulness paired with His mercy that overflows even at the depth of judgment’s consequences.

etymology: Hebrew chōmer, “a heap, large quantity,” from chāmar (to heap up); the largest Hebrew dry measure, equal to ten ephahs (approximately 6.5 bushels / 220 liters). Not to be confused with the Greek poet Homer.
biblical_def: The homer (Hebrew chōmer, “a heap”) is the largest dry measure in the Hebrew system—ten ephahs, approximately 6.5 bushels or 220 liters of grain. The word appears across the OT in contexts of substantial agricultural reckoning, prophetic measurement, and the divinely-prescribed sacrificial offerings. Several major uses anchor the doctrine. First, the quail-providence in the wilderness: Numbers 11:32 records that, when the LORD answered the people’s craving for flesh by sending quails, he that gathered least gathered ten homers: and they spread them all abroad for themselves round about the camp. Even the least-energetic gatherer collected ten homers of quail—an immense quantity, illustrating the overwhelming abundance of the provision that nonetheless was followed by judgment (the plague at Kibroth-hattaavah for the people’s lusting). Second, the Levitical agricultural standards. Leviticus 27:16 prescribes the valuation of a field according to its seed: an homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver. The homer is the standard measuring-unit for agricultural reckoning of crops, land, and tribute. Third, the prophetic messages. Hosea 3:2 records the prophet’s purchase of his adulterous wife Gomer for fifteen pieces of silver, an homer of barley, and a half-homer of barley—a substantial price reflecting the seriousness of the redemption-figure. Isaiah 5:10 prophesies coming judgment in agricultural terms: yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah—the catastrophic crop-failure of judgment, where the seed sown is ten times what is harvested. Ezekiel 45:11, 14 prescribe the measurement-standards for the prophetic temple vision, with the homer as the standard. Fourth, the symbolic-prophetic. Hosea 7:8: Ephraim is a cake not turned; the imagery is bread-related, the unit-context grain-measurement, the substance the prophetic indictment of Israel’s incomplete-conversion (a cake baked on one side, raw on the other—externally religious, internally unrepentant). The homer therefore serves several biblical-narrative-and-prophetic functions: the large standard unit for agricultural reckoning, the measuring-figure for divine provision-or-judgment, the prophetic standard for crop-yield warnings, and the larger context for various symbolic uses. As with the other biblical weights and measures, the homer is no mere agricultural curiosity but the standardized measurement-unit on which the LORD’s precise prescriptions for sacrifice, tribute, and just commerce all depend.

EPHAH, n. — A Hebrew dry-measure, approximately 22 liters; one-tenth of a homer.

corruption_summary: The homer as a biblical unit is corrupted in modern reading chiefly by being treated as quaint agricultural detail without operative theological substance—missing the structural use of the homer across the prophetic, sacrificial, and narrative literature as the standardized measurement-unit on which God’s precise prescriptions for sacrifice, tribute, and prophetic warning depend.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers tend to convert biblical weights and measures into approximate modern equivalents and skip the precision the OT writers preserved. The homer is one of many such units (ephah, bath, hin, log, seah, cab, omer, etc.) that contemporary preaching tends to treat as quaint agricultural curiosity without operative significance. The biblical writers used these units with deliberate precision: when Isaiah 5:10 says the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah, the prophetic-judgment severity depends on the reader knowing that an ephah is one-tenth of a homer, so the announcement is of a ten-to-one crop failure—catastrophic agricultural collapse as covenant judgment. When Leviticus 27:16 sets the valuation at fifty shekels for a homer of barley seed, the actual price-equivalent of a substantial agricultural transaction is being specified with precision. When Numbers 11:32 records that he that gathered least gathered ten homers of quail, the overwhelming abundance of the provision is being conveyed in concrete units. The recovery is the recovery of the precision, with the modern reader paying attention to the standardized units the OT writers used and reading the prophetic-and-narrative substance more fully because of the attention.

The deeper substance is the OT theology of standardized measurement as the infrastructure of just commerce, accurate prophetic warning, and precise sacrificial obedience. The homer’s large-unit reckoning was no less precision-bound than the gerah’s small-unit weight; the LORD’s holiness extended to both ends of the measurement scale, requiring just balances and accurate measures throughout. The contemporary application of this measurement-theology is broader than weights-and-measures-ethics narrowly considered: it teaches that God’s holiness extends to the precision of every transaction, every promise, every commitment, every account. The saint’s integrity is to be precision-shaped, not approximation-shaped. The homer-precision of OT agricultural reckoning has its New Covenant analog in the saint’s commitment to precise honesty in every dimension of his stewardship and witness—a precision that mirrors the God who measured both gerahs and homers with equal exactness.

etymology: Old English spann, the distance between the outstretched thumb and little finger of a man’s hand (approximately 9 inches / 23 cm); a Hebrew small-linear-measure equal to half a cubit. Hebrew zēreth.
biblical_def: The span is the small Hebrew linear measure equal to half a cubit (approximately 9 inches / 23 cm)—the distance between the outstretched thumb and little finger of a man’s hand when the palm is spread. Several biblical uses anchor the doctrine. First, the literal: Exodus 28:16 and 39:9 prescribe the breastplate of judgment as foursquare and doubled; a span shall be the length thereof, and a span shall be the breadth thereof—a 9-inch square doubled to make a pouch holding the Urim and Thummim. The span is the precise dimension of the high priest’s breastplate. 1 Samuel 17:4 records the height of Goliath as six cubits and a span—approximately 9 feet 9 inches (depending on which cubit-standard is used), specifying the giant’s exact stature in the most easily-visualized small unit. The literal uses establish the span as a familiar everyday measurement, the hand-spread distance that any Israelite could verify against his own hand. Second, the figurative-prophetic. Isaiah 40:12 is the great use: who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance? The rhetorical question sets the LORD’s incomparable greatness against human smallness: the LORD measures the heavens themselves with a span—the same 9-inch hand-spread by which the Israelite measured his garment-cloth, applied by the divine hand to the very dimensions of the heavens. The figure is one of Scripture’s most striking expressions of God’s incomparable greatness; the smallness of the everyday human span is contrasted with the greatness of the God to whom even the heavens are span-measurable. Third, the human-life-brevity register. Psalm 39:5 (David’s great psalm of human frailty): behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. The handbreadth (a smaller unit than the span; approximately 3 inches) and the span here function as figures of the brevity of human life from the divine perspective. The believer’s life, measured against eternity, is a handbreadth—a span at most. The figure invites the saint to number his days, to apply his heart to wisdom, and to live with eternity in view rather than to be deceived by the apparent largeness of the span-length of his present life. The span as a biblical unit therefore serves both literal (architectural and bodily measurements) and figurative (the LORD’s greatness, the brevity of life) functions; its everyday-familiarity makes it a particularly effective vehicle for both kinds of biblical teaching.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPAN as the space from the end of the thumb to the end of the little finger, when extended; nine inches; the eighth of a fathom; in scripture, both a literal small-linear-measure (Goliath’s height, the high priest’s breastplate) and figuratively the standard by which God measures the heavens (Isa 40:12) and by which the brevity of human life is conveyed (Ps 39:5).
webster_full: SPAN, n. — The space from the end of the thumb to the end of the little finger, when extended; the eighth of a fathom; nine inches.
HANDBREADTH, n. — A measure of three or four inches; the breadth of the hand; used figuratively in Ps 39:5 of the brevity of human life.

corruption_summary: The span as a biblical unit is corrupted in modern reading chiefly by being converted to inches and skipped past, losing the rhetorical force of Isaiah 40:12’s contrast (the same span by which men measure cloth is the unit by which God measures heaven) and the pastoral weight of Psalm 39:5’s handbreadth-image of life’s brevity.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern conversion of biblical measurements into inches-and-centimeters often muffles the rhetorical force the biblical writers built into their figures. Isaiah 40:12’s use of span is one of the most striking examples. The Israelite hearer knew the span: it was the everyday measurement he used for cloth, for room-dimensions, for the small distances of daily life. To hear that the LORD meted out heaven with the span—the same span the hearer used for ordinary measurements—was to encounter the incomparable greatness of God in a register the smallest household economy could vividly grasp. The modern translation that converts span to handbreadths or to 9-inch units loses the immediate connection to the hearer’s own hand-spread. The recovery is the recovery of the figure: the same hand-distance by which the saint measures his garment is the unit by which God measures heaven; the smallness of the human span against the greatness of the divine application sets the LORD’s incomparable greatness in sharpest relief.

Psalm 39:5’s use of the handbreadth carries similar pastoral substance. Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth—David measures the length of his life against the smallest familiar unit, and finds that his days, even at his best state, are as nothing before God. The figure is meant to produce the wisdom-effect of Psalm 90:12: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. The contemporary believer who lives as if the span-length of his present life were a large amount of time has missed the perspective the handbreadth-figure intends to teach. The recovery is the recovery of the figure’s force: my life, measured against eternity, is a handbreadth; my best years are a span; the soberness of this measurement should drive me to apply my heart to wisdom while the brief span remains. The span and handbreadth as biblical units are therefore not chiefly numismatic or architectural curiosities but the vivid figures by which Scripture teaches both the greatness of God and the brevity of life—each in the smallest unit the everyday hand provides.
roots_summary: Hebrew zēreth (span); a small linear measure (half a cubit, approximately 9 inches); used literally for the high priest’s breastplate and Goliath’s height, and figuratively for the LORD’s span-measurement of heaven (Isa 40:12) and the handbreadth-brevity of human life (Ps 39:5).
roots_lines: Hebrew zēreth (H2239) — span (7 OT uses; Ex 28:16; 39:9; 1 Sam 17:4; Isa 40:12; Ezek 43:13).
Hebrew tōphach / tephach (H2947, H2948) — handbreadth (a smaller unit, approximately 3 inches; Ex 25:25; 1 Kgs 7:26; Ps 39:5).
Hebrew ’ammāh (H520) — cubit (the larger linear unit; 2 spans make 1 cubit).
Hebrew zēreth-cognates in Akkadian and other Semitic languages — the span as a widespread ancient-Near-Eastern unit based on the hand-spread.
usage: Meted out heaven with the span—Isa 40:12’s incomparable-greatness figure: the same hand-distance by which men measure cloth is the unit by which God measures the heavens.
Thou hast made my days as an handbreadth—Ps 39:5’s pastoral figure of life’s brevity, measured against eternity.

Modern conversion to inches loses the rhetorical force; recovery is the figure in its everyday-familiarity: the span is the hand-spread the hearer himself uses, and its application to heaven and to human life carries the substantive force the biblical writers intended.

etymology: Old English furlang, “furrow-long,” the length of a furrow in a field; in modern terms, one-eighth of a mile (220 yards / 201 meters). The KJV uses furlong for the Greek stadion, the standard Greco-Roman unit of approximately 600 feet / 185 meters.
biblical_def: The furlong (Greek stadion) is the standard Greco-Roman unit of distance used across the New Testament for the measurement of distances between places, the dimensions of large objects, and (most strikingly) the dimensions of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21. Several biblical uses anchor the doctrine. First, the distance-from-Jerusalem of various NT events. Luke 24:13: the village of Emmaus, to which the two disciples were walking on the day of Christ’s resurrection, was threescore furlongs (60 stadia, approximately 7 miles) from Jerusalem. John 6:19: the disciples in the boat at the storm-on-the-lake had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs (25-30 stadia, approximately 3-3.5 miles) when they saw Jesus walking on the water. John 11:18: Bethany, where Lazarus was raised, was nigh unto Jerusalem, about fifteen furlongs off (15 stadia, approximately 2 miles). Each gives the precise distance for the historical-narrative reader. Second, the dimensions of large-scale eschatological objects. Revelation 14:20 records the bloody outcome of the apocalyptic harvest: and the winepress was trodden without the city, and blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles, by the space of a thousand and six hundred furlongs—1,600 stadia (approximately 200 miles), an immense extent representing the comprehensive nature of the eschatological judgment. Third, and supremely, the dimensions of the New Jerusalem. Revelation 21:16: and the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal. The New Jerusalem is described as a perfect cube of 12,000 stadia per side—approximately 1,500 miles per side, an immense city echoing the perfect-cube-shape of the most holy place in tabernacle and temple (which was a 10-cubit cube in the tabernacle, 20-cubit cube in Solomon’s temple). The New Jerusalem is, in its very dimensions, the consummate holy of holies: the place where God’s presence dwells perfectly with His people, with no temple in the city because the LORD God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it. The 12,000-stadia measurement is therefore not numerical decoration but the consummate eschatological architectural figure of the perfect dwelling-place of God with His redeemed. The furlong as a biblical unit therefore serves both the historical-narrative function (precise distances for events) and the apocalyptic-eschatological function (the immense dimensions of the consummate city).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FURLONG as a measure of length, the eighth of a mile; in scripture, the KJV renders the Greek stadion as furlong, used for distances (Emmaus 60 furlongs from Jerusalem) and for the immense dimensions of the New Jerusalem (12,000 furlongs per side, Rev 21:16).
webster_full: FURLONG, n. — A measure of length; the eighth of a mile; forty rods, poles, or perches. In scripture, the KJV renders the Greek stadion as furlong; the standard Greco-Roman unit of approximately 600 feet.
STADION (Greek) — The standard Greco-Roman unit of distance, approximately 600 feet / 185 meters; named for the stadia of the Greek athletic games.

corruption_summary: The furlong-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the modern translation drift that has substituted miles or stadia for the KJV’s furlong—and on the other (more significantly) by the over-spiritualization of the Revelation 21:16 dimensions of the New Jerusalem that treats the 12,000 furlongs as merely symbolic without the substantive architectural-eschatological connection to the holy-of-holies-as-perfect-cube pattern Scripture itself maintains.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern translations have variously rendered stadion as mile (approximate equivalent), stadia (Greek transliteration), or specific-distance equivalents (two miles off for the 15 stadia of John 11:18). Each has its rationale; each loses something the KJV’s furlong preserves: the precise unit-name that lets the reader track the specific measurements as the biblical writers gave them. The furlong-precision matters especially in Revelation, where the apocalyptic visions use specific numerical figures (the 1,600 furlongs of Rev 14:20; the 12,000 furlongs of Rev 21:16) that are themselves part of the symbolic substance the visions convey. The recovery is the recovery of attention to the precise units, with the modern reader paying enough attention to the numerical detail to engage the symbolic substance the apocalyptic-and-narrative measurements carry.

The deeper substance is the New-Jerusalem-as-consummate-holy-of-holies pattern Revelation 21:16 conveys. The city is described as a perfect cube of 12,000 furlongs per side—immensely larger than any earthly city, and significantly cube-shaped, with length, breadth, and height equal. The cube-shape echoes the holy of holies of the tabernacle (a perfect 10-cubit cube, Ex 26:33 by inference; Lev 16:14-15 in priestly use) and of Solomon’s temple (a perfect 20-cubit cube, 1 Kgs 6:20: and the oracle in the forepart was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in the height thereof). The consummate New Jerusalem of Rev 21 is therefore the eschatological holy of holies—the perfect dwelling-place of God with His redeemed, no longer a small inner room in a larger sanctuary but the entire city, into which the redeemed enter and where the LORD God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple. The furlong-measurements of 12,000 per side, and the explicit length and breadth and height of it are equal, are the architectural-symbolic figures the apocalyptic vision uses to convey the consummate eschatological reality: the holy of holies expanded to encompass the entire city of God’s redeemed people, with no veil, no separation, no inaccessible inner chamber—only the perpetual presence of God with His people in the perfect-cube city forever.
